pitch-cities.promise: Play GTA in the real cities that inspired it, with a different challenge in each city.
how: Start in Los Angeles, then travel through the selected GTA-inspired cities.
In each city, match one recognizable game location and complete one local challenge.
Finish in Miami with the hardest challenge and a ranking of the cities.
intro: ALEX
I’m playing GTA in every city that inspired it.
Start beside one landmark, then match it to the game version.
ALAN
But in every city, we have to complete a challenge from the game in real life.
Show three quick city/challenge pairings.
ALEX
First stop: Los Angeles. And we’re already late.
Begin the first challenge; explain its deadline in the action.
turn: ALAN
That worked in the game. It definitely didn’t work here.
Cut from the game plan to the real attempt when that contrast actually happens.
payoff: ALEX
We’ve made it to the final city. One challenge left.
Finish the Miami challenge, then reveal which city delivered the best experience.
packaging: A familiar franchise × a real-world travel mission.
One twin, one iconic landmark and its matching game version.
The game/real-life contrast explains the idea before someone reads the title.
pitch-cities.support: Travel and game/real-life references support the ingredients. The exact multi-city GTA format remains a new test.
refs: A recognizable real-world activity makes a technology/game premise accessible.
A journey has a clear destination; this source was below its nearby-upload median.

pitch-car.promise: Win a game race and leave with the matching real car.
how: Pair each driver with an in-game replica of a real prize car.
Run a short qualifier, then one escalating final race.
Hand the winner the actual keys after the finish.
intro: ALEX
Win this race, and you keep this car.
Put the real car and its keys in the first shot.
ALAN
Everyone is racing the exact car they could drive home today.
Match each contestant’s game car to the real version.
ALEX
Three laps. One winner. Go!
Start the race immediately.
turn: ALAN
You can take the safe route—or risk the shortcut.
Reveal the shortcut when the leading drivers reach it.
payoff: ALEX
You won the race. These are yours.
Show the finish, hand over the keys and capture the first reaction in the real car.
packaging: A simple action → a tangible reward.
One red car, oversized keys and a delighted twin.
The physical prize makes the stakes easy to understand without game knowledge.
pitch-car.support: Car spectacle and keep-the-prize examples support the package; the race-to-real-car conversion is the new hook.
refs: One fast car makes the game challenge instantly legible.
The main-channel reference connects a simple challenge with a real car reward.

pitch-rooms.promise: Build a secret room in each selected game and see whether the other twin can find them.
how: Give GTA, Minecraft and Roblox one distinctive hidden room each.
Let the other twin search without knowing where the entrances are.
Finish with the biggest room and reveal how each entrance was hidden.
intro: ALEX
I built a secret room in every one of these video games.
Open one ordinary-looking wall into a spectacular room.
ALAN
And I have to find all of them before the timer runs out.
Show the three game worlds and the search timer.
ALEX
Your first room is somewhere in this house. Good luck.
Start the search while the hidden twin watches.
turn: ALEX
You just walked right past it.
Hold on the missed entrance, then let the search continue.
payoff: ALAN
There is no way this was under us the whole time.
Reveal the final room and replay the moment the searcher nearly found it.
packaging: A proven Stokes subject × familiar game worlds.
A tiny entrance reveals one huge, bright room.
The image supplies the hidden reveal; the title supplies the cross-game scale.
pitch-rooms.support: The main-channel secret-room references give a close subject match. The game version is an adaptation, not a measured CTR improvement.
refs: Direct Stokes secret-room subject and discovery promise.
Large hidden interiors and multiple reveals support the visual format.

pitch-hunters.promise: The twins must reach an extraction point while 100 GTA hunters try to stop them.
how: Give the twins a destination and a short head start.
Let the hunters close routes as the twins change their escape plan.
End with one last push to the extraction point.
intro: ALEX
These 100 hunters have one job: stop us from escaping GTA.
Show the hunters, then the twins beside their getaway car.
ALAN
If we reach that helicopter, we win. If they catch both of us, we lose.
Reveal the extraction point in the distance.
ALEX
They’re coming. Get in!
Begin the escape at the countdown.
turn: ALAN
They’ve blocked the road. We need another way out.
Use the first route closure to force a new plan.
payoff: ALEX
We’re not leaving without both of us.
Resolve the final rescue and show whether the twins make extraction.
packaging: A tiny team versus an overwhelming force.
One small getaway car against a wall of pursuers.
The imbalance creates the question: how could the twins escape?
pitch-hunters.support: GTA hunters and large player manhunts are close format references, with two different game-channel examples above their source baselines.
refs: A large player army makes the odds visible.

pitch-disasters.promise: Every minute, another disaster changes how the twins can survive the GTA city.
how: Start with one simple disaster and a visible countdown.
Stack a new hazard every minute so each escape creates the next problem.
Make the final safe location the last destination.
intro: ALEX
Every minute, another disaster happens in GTA.
Show the first timer turning over as the city changes.
ALAN
We have to survive until the final disaster—and that car is our only way out.
Show the car and a quick glimpse of the biggest hazard.
ALEX
The water is already rising. Drive!
Start the first escape with water entering the route.
turn: ALAN
The road’s gone. Head for the roof.
A new disaster removes the plan that was working.
payoff: ALEX
This is the last safe place in the city.
Bring the remaining hazards together for one final escape or defeat.
packaging: Survival × a repeating escalation rule.
A tiny escape vehicle beneath one enormous disaster.
The title explains the escalation; the picture shows the size of the problem.
pitch-disasters.support: World-changing hazards and long-form survival both have public reference support. The one-minute GTA escalation is a proposed combination.
refs: A flood changes the world and forces new decisions.
A sustained survival objective gives escalating danger a destination.

pitch-life.promise: Let GTA decide what the twins do in real life for one day.
how: Connect game choices to real meals, transport, clothing and activities.
Reveal each real-life consequence only when the game makes the choice.
End with the biggest choice of the day and both twins’ verdict.
intro: ALEX
For the next 24 hours, GTA controls our real lives.
Match a game action to its real-life consequence.
ALAN
Whatever we eat, wear or drive in the game, we have to do in real life.
Show three fast examples, each clearly different.
ALEX
So first, the game is choosing our breakfast.
Start the first choice before explaining the rest of the day.
turn: ALAN
Please don’t choose that one.
Pause on the choice before revealing what the game selects.
payoff: ALEX
GTA gets one final decision. Then we get our lives back.
Resolve the final activity and compare the best and worst choices.
packaging: Loss of control × a familiar franchise × a fixed day.
One game choice causes one surprising real-life result.
The contrast gives non-gamers a reason to watch the outcome.
pitch-life.support: Stokes has an existing life-controlled-for-a-day format. Game chaos supplies an adjacent escalation reference.
refs: Repeated game changes create new problems without changing the core promise.

pitch-experiments.promise: Find out how large a barrier it takes to stop GTA’s train.
how: Begin with a small car barrier and a real collision.
Increase the number and improve the barrier after each result.
End with the full 10,000-car attempt and a clear answer.
intro: ALEX
Can 10,000 cars stop a train in GTA?
Put the train opposite the enormous car wall.
ALAN
We’re starting with ten. And every time the train wins, the wall gets bigger.
Show the first small barrier next to the final scale.
ALEX
Here comes the train.
Play the first impact through to its result.
turn: ALAN
More cars didn’t work. What if we change the shape?
Let the last failure lead directly to the next design.
payoff: ALEX
This is the 10,000-car test. Can anything stop it?
Show the entire final collision, then state the answer.
packaging: A giant number × a simple yes/no experiment.
One unstoppable train facing one enormous wall of cars.
The thumbnail turns the question into an immediately readable collision.
pitch-experiments.support: Large-scale experiment and destruction references support spectacle. Their views do not establish that the specific train test will win.
refs: One oversized experiment makes a clear visual promise.
A spectacular final test rewards the scale promised in the package.

pitch-killer.promise: One hidden killer is inside a group of 100 players, and the twins must find them before time runs out.
how: Give one player the hidden role and introduce the twins as investigators.
Let each round reveal one new clue and one meaningful accusation.
End with a final vote and a replay of the clues that exposed the killer.
intro: ALEX
One of these 100 players is secretly the killer.
Show the crowd, then one obscured suspect among them.
ALAN
We have to find them before they take out the entire lobby.
Establish the player counter and the first clue.
ALEX
Everybody freeze. Where were you when this happened?
Start the first investigation immediately.
turn: ALAN
That story doesn’t match the footage.
Put the accusation beside the clue that contradicts it.
payoff: ALEX
We’re locking in our final vote.
Reveal the killer and replay their earlier choices from the new perspective.
packaging: A large group × one hidden threat.
The twins investigate a crowd with one concealed red silhouette.
A single secret makes the audience play along with every accusation.
pitch-killer.support: The strongest reference is a 100-player social-deduction game; murder-mystery packaging provides a second route into the premise.
refs: A recognizable creator mystery creates an immediate question.

pitch-course.promise: The crew tries to beat an absurd GTA course that becomes harder at every stage.
how: Show the final obstacle, then begin at the first checkpoint.
Give each new section a different skill and a clear consequence for failure.
Bring the closest competitors together for the last crossing.
intro: ALEX
We built the most impossible obstacle course in GTA.
Reveal the entire course, with the final gap clearly visible.
ALAN
We have to get from here to that finish line without skipping a single obstacle.
Trace the simple route from start to finish.
ALEX
The first jump looks easy. You go first.
Start the first attempt and keep its result.
turn: ALAN
You only get one chance at this checkpoint.
Introduce the final high-stakes section after viewers understand the course.
payoff: ALEX
One jump left. Don’t look down.
Let the decisive attempt finish before the celebration or failure reaction.
packaging: An impossible superlative × an obvious finish line.
One tiny player/car facing one enormous suspended course.
The scale difference explains the difficulty without a rules lecture.
pitch-course.support: Impossible-maze and layered-escape references support progression and an earned finish; the GTA course is the new execution.
refs: A huge playable challenge with a clear completion goal.
Each new layer gives the audience a reason to see what comes next.

pitch-steal.promise: Complete increasingly difficult GTA heists to win matching real prizes.
how: Begin with a small, clearly stated real reward.
Move from an easy theft to a guarded target, then the biggest prize.
Award only the prizes attached to completed game challenges.
intro: ALEX
Anything you steal in GTA today, you get to keep in real life.
Match a game object to the real prize beside it.
ALAN
The better the prize, the harder the heist.
Reveal three prize levels, with the largest last.
ALEX
Your first target is parked right there.
Start the first theft and reveal the obstacle on approach.
turn: ALAN
You can keep what you’ve won—or try for the biggest prize.
Put the secured rewards beside the final target.
payoff: ALEX
You got it out. Now it’s yours.
Resolve the final heist, then hand over the matching real reward.
packaging: An unrestricted-sounding action × a tangible keep-it reward.
One GTA target paired with the matching real prize.
The audience understands what the contestant wants and why the risk grows.
pitch-steal.support: Risk/reward and game-build-to-real-prize examples support the ingredients. Theft-specific thumbnail art is still a separate packaging task.
refs: A bigger reward makes the next risk a meaningful decision.
The game result can lead to a concrete real-world payoff.

pitch-prison.promise: The twins build a GTA prison, then challenge their friends to escape it.
how: Reveal the prison’s main defenses and the escape objective.
Let the escape team test plans against each security layer.
Finish with one coordinated attempt while the builders defend.
intro: ALEX
I created the world’s most secure prison in GTA.
Reveal the prison with one enormous, obvious defense.
ALAN
And our friends have to escape it before the timer runs out.
Introduce the escape team inside its starting cell.
ALEX
Your time starts now.
Show their first escape plan immediately.
turn: ALAN
They found a way through. Lock down the next section.
Use a successful escape step to expose a new defense.
payoff: ALEX
This is the last door between you and freedom.
Resolve the final escape attempt and compare the winning plan with the original prison design.
packaging: A superlative build × an escape challenge.
One towering prison, a tiny exit and the twins as opposing sides.
The title establishes the claim; the attempted escape tests it.
pitch-prison.support: Prison and impossible-escape references support the challenge. The new angle makes the twins the builders as well as the hosts.
refs: A simple escape objective can sustain a sequence of changing barriers.
An extraordinary prison location adds a clear visual twist.

pitch-minecraft-halo.promise: 100 Minecrafters face 100 Halo players in a community-versus-community showdown, with a twin captaining each side.
how: Give each 100-player community one twin as its captain in a shared challenge arena.
Run a building round and a shooting round; each earns an advantage for the finale.
End in one huge capture-the-base battle that decides the winning community.
intro: ALEX
These are 100 Minecrafters. And these are 100 Halo players.
Reveal the two armies in matching wide shots, then their captains.
ALAN
Today, we’re finding out which gaming community is better—builders or shooters.
Show one spectacular build and one coordinated Halo-style attack.
ALEX
I’ve got the Halo players. Alan’s got Minecraft. Let the first challenge begin.
Start the building round with both teams racing toward the same objective.
turn: ALAN
You won on your game. Now let’s see what happens on ours.
Switch from the builders’ home-field round to the shooters’ round, carrying the score forward.
payoff: ALEX
No more practice rounds. First team to capture that base wins.
Bring the earned advantages into the final battle, then celebrate the actual winning community.
packaging: 100 [community] vs 100 [community]—the boys-versus-girls structure with gaming identities.
Two equally imposing armies, Minecraft versus Halo, with Alan and Alex as the captains.
The rivalry is understandable to the main-channel audience; each community has someone to support.
pitch-minecraft-halo.support: Two large MrBeast team competitions support the main-channel rivalry package. The Minecraft/Halo matchup is the new variation.
refs: Two familiar identities and equal-sized teams make the sides immediately clear.
Contrasting strengths give both teams a reason to win different challenges.

pitch-civilizations.promise: Invite top players from selected game communities to build civilizations and find out which community can rule the shared world.
how: Begin with equal-sized communities and starting territories; proposed games are Minecraft, Halo, GTA and Fortnite.
Let them build cities, choose leaders, trade, make alliances and handle one shared crisis.
Open the borders for a final contest over the central capital; the civilization that holds it wins.
intro: ALEX
I brought the best players from these video games into one world to build their own civilizations.
Reveal the proposed game communities and their separate starting territories.
ALAN
They can build cities, make alliances, or go to war. But only one civilization can rule this world.
Show a fast tease of one city, one negotiation and one battle.
ALEX
Players, choose your leaders. Your civilization starts now.
Drop into the first community’s real decision and introduce a leader to follow.
turn: ALAN
The borders are opening. Are you making peace—or preparing for war?
Let the communities’ choices drive the alliances and the conflict; follow the leaders’ actual decisions.
payoff: ALEX
The capital is open. Whoever holds it at the end rules the world.
Resolve the final contest, name the winning civilization and show what happened to the others.
packaging: I simulated [recognizable communities] as civilizations → which one wins?
A large civilization map with two dominant, visibly different game empires and the twins presenting it.
Game identity supplies instant contrast; the civilization story supplies leaders, alliances and an outcome.
pitch-civilizations.support: Civilization videos on two channels show audience interest in community-led stories. The cross-game community mix is the new variation.
refs: Contrasting starting communities create different societies and leaders to follow.
A familiar rivalry carries a civilization story through alliances and a final conflict.

idea-multiverse.promise: The crew races through a shared adventure built from their favorite games; last place takes a pickle dunk.
how: Open overhead with Alex, Alan, Kat, Tanner and Shawn at their stations, then choose characters and vehicles.
Race from Rainbow Road through GTA City, the Nether and the End staging area into space; arrivals collect chests and keep moving.
Resolve the final space challenge, reveal the actual standings and deliver the pickle dunk.
intro: ALEX
THIS is the world’s greatest video game.
Start overhead with the crew standing at their PCs, then show one clear crossover moment.
ALAN
We put our favorite games into the same adventure. And last place takes a pickle dunk.
Show the route and the real dunk payoff, then sit into the stations.
CAST
Can we choose a different punishment?
Reveal the character/vehicle choices and begin the countdown.
turn: ALEX
First one here gets the gold chest. Everyone else, choose carefully.
Let the first arrival open the gold chest while the others are still racing; reveal the next game-world surprise.
payoff: ALAN
Last place has one final challenge—in real life.
Return from the space finale, reveal the actual standings, then show the pickle dunk and the crew’s reaction.
packaging: A superlative game promise × recognizable crossovers × a real-life consequence.
One impossible game collision and one strong twin reaction.
The first shot pays off the title; the route and punishment tell viewers why to stay.
idea-multiverse.support: The opening and route follow the October 23 production script. Public spectacle/race references support individual ingredients; there is no episode-specific CTR result.
refs: A recognizable game spectacle can be presented as one large visual idea.
A readable race objective supports the competitive opening.

idea-launch-gta-prank.promise: Convince Alex he is playing an early version of GTA 6, then escalate the absurdities until the reveal.
how: Present the setup as an apparent early-game opportunity and let Alex take the controller.
Begin with believable play, then introduce increasingly strange missions and characters.
Let the clues build to a clear reveal of how the prank was made.

Alex thinks he’s about to play GTA 6. But we built this entire game to prank him.
Show Alex arriving, then a quick behind-the-scenes glimpse for the audience.
ALAN
Every mission, every character, and every surprise is controlled by us.
Tease two strange moments without revealing his biggest reaction.
ALAN
Alex, come try this.
Let him sit down and begin the first believable mission.
turn: ALAN
Let’s see how long it takes him to notice this.
Introduce the next clue after Alex has committed to the mission.
payoff: ALAN
Alex, there’s something we need to tell you.
Reveal the prank, show how it was built and let Alex react.

Alex’s reaction to one unexpected GTA-style scene; the audience gets the prank context in the opening.

idea-launch-gta-prank.support: Stokes prank history and controlled-game surprises support the structure. No actual Rockstar leak or endorsement is part of the pitch.
refs: A direct Stokes prank identity and escalating surprises.
A creator secretly changing the game supplies an adjacent prank mechanism.

idea-launch-gta6.promise: The boys stay in one room until someone finishes GTA 6, while guests join for complete standalone challenges.
how: Start the room challenge and establish the agreed game finish point.
Follow the leading run, the setbacks and guest mission blocks while post receives finished segments.
When the first player finishes, release everyone and resolve the room story.

We’re locked in this room until one of us beats GTA 6.
Show the occupied stations, the room and the game starting.
ALAN
The first person to finish gets everyone out. And we’ve invited some help.

Start the game. Let’s see who gets us out first.

The twins in a visibly used gaming room, with one obvious exit and the game as context.

idea-launch-gta6.support: Closed-goal survival and competitive gaming references support the ingredients. Guest appearances and the final recording duration remain unconfirmed.
refs: A single survival/completion goal carries a long progression.
Clear GTA objectives and player reactions keep the game story accessible.

idea-01.promise: Put the cheapest and most extravagant options through the same tests and find out what the extra value changes.

Run three matched tests with visible results.
Reveal which one won each test and whether the expensive option was worth it.

One cheap option beside one outrageous premium version.
